WHY FUEL PLANNING MATTERS
Safety First

Running out of fuel isn’t an option. Plan ahead and stay in control.

Weather Changes Everything

Wind, current, and sea state can significantly impact fuel burn.

Plan With Reserve

Build in reserve so you have options when conditions or plans change.

How Much Fuel Does a Boat Use Per Hour?

Boat fuel use is usually measured in gallons per hour, or GPH. There is no single GPH number that applies to every boat of a certain length or horsepower. Fuel burn changes with engine RPM and load, the hull, boat weight, propeller, trim, weather, current, sea state and other operating conditions.

The best number to use for trip planning is your boat's actual fuel burn at the speed you expect to cruise. If your engine display or fuel-flow system provides real-time GPH, use that value. Manufacturer performance tests for your specific boat and engine combination are the next-best reference.

Fuel burn can rise much faster than speed

One manufacturer test example: Yamaha tested a 23-foot Sportsman Open 232 with a single 300-hp F300 outboard. At 3,500 RPM the boat ran 27.2 mph while burning 8.3 GPH, or 3.28 MPG. At 5,800 RPM it ran 48.4 mph while burning 26.4 GPH, or 1.83 MPG.

In that test, speed increased about 78%, while hourly fuel consumption increased about 218%. That is why wide-open-throttle fuel burn should not be used as a substitute for actual cruising fuel burn.

Yamaha test data. This is one manufacturer test example, not a prediction for other boats.

Real Boat Fuel-Burn Examples

These manufacturer performance tests show how fuel burn and fuel economy vary among specific boat and engine combinations at specific test RPM settings.

Manufacturer boat fuel-burn test examples
BOAT / ENGINE	TEST RPM	SPEED	FUEL BURN	FUEL ECONOMY	SOURCE

G3 Boats 15 DLX / Yamaha F40
40 hp single outboard
	4,000 RPM	18.4 MPH	1.5 GPH	12.27 MPG	Yamaha test data

Crestliner 1850 Fish Hawk / Mercury 150 Pro XS
150 hp single outboard
	3,000 RPM	21.3 MPH	3.6 GPH	6.0 MPG	Mercury test data

Sportsman Open 232 / Yamaha F300
300 hp single outboard
	3,500 RPM	27.2 MPH	8.3 GPH	3.28 MPG	Yamaha test data

Sea Hunt Gamefish 30 CB / Twin Yamaha F350
Twin 350 hp outboards
	3,500 RPM	35.9 MPH	17.2 GPH total	2.09 MPG	Yamaha test data

These are examples, not lookup values for your boat. Manufacturer performance tests are conducted with specific hulls, loads, propellers and conditions. Your boat's actual fuel burn may be different.

GPH vs. MPG: What the Numbers Mean
GPH — Gallons Per Hour

GPH tells you how quickly the engines are consuming fuel. If your boat burns 8 GPH for three hours, the trip consumes about 24 gallons before reserve or other adjustments.

Fuel Used = Running Hours × GPH
MPG — Miles Per Gallon

MPG measures how far the boat travels for each gallon burned. A higher GPH does not automatically mean worse fuel economy if the boat is also traveling substantially faster.

MPG = Speed in MPH ÷ GPH
Nautical Miles Per Gallon

When working in knots and nautical miles, the same idea can be expressed as nautical miles per gallon.

NM per Gallon = Speed in Knots ÷ GPH

For trip planning, GPH tells you the burn rate while distance-per-gallon measurements help identify the more economical cruising point.

Why Boat Fuel Consumption Changes With Speed

Boat fuel consumption does not increase in a simple one-to-one relationship with speed. As speed and engine load change, the hull's resistance through the water, running attitude and propulsion efficiency also change.

On a planing boat, efficiency can change significantly as the boat transitions onto plane and then continues toward higher RPM. More throttle normally increases gallons per hour, but the most useful efficiency measurement is how much distance the boat travels for each gallon consumed.

This is why the lowest GPH is not automatically the best cruising speed. Idling may burn very little fuel per hour but cover very little distance. At the other extreme, high RPM can dramatically increase GPH without providing a proportional increase in speed.

How to Find Your Boat's Actual GPH
Use onboard fuel-flow data

If your engine display, multifunction display or fuel-management system reports real-time GPH, use that data while operating at your normal cruising speed.

Yamaha states that its engine-management systems can continuously calculate fuel consumption and display information that lets operators evaluate fuel economy while underway.

Find a manufacturer performance bulletin

Search for a performance test matching your boat model, engine, horsepower and engine count. These reports commonly show RPM, speed, GPH and MPG at multiple throttle settings.

Yamaha Performance Bulletins

Compare with your own operating history

Fuel added, engine hours and trip records can help establish a real-world baseline when the operating profile is reasonably consistent.

One mixed-use tank does not automatically produce an accurate cruising GPH number.

Use a conservative estimate when necessary

If measured or manufacturer data is unavailable, use a conservative planning value and maintain additional reserve until you have enough real-world data to refine it.

Once you know your expected cruise GPH, enter it in the FloatPlanWizard calculator above along with distance, speed and reserve assumptions.

What Affects Boat Fuel Consumption?
Boat & Load
Passengers
Gear
Fuel and water carried
Optional equipment
Overall operating weight

More weight generally requires more power to achieve and maintain a given operating condition.

Hull & Running Surface
Hull design
Bottom condition
Fouling
Bottom paint
Added drag

Hull condition and drag affect how much power is required to move the boat through the water.

Engine, Propeller & Trim
Engine RPM and load
Propeller selection and condition
Engine trim
Trim tabs where applicable
Engine condition

Propeller setup and trim affect the boat's running attitude and how efficiently engine power is converted into forward motion.

Conditions & Route
Wind
Current
Waves and sea state
No-wake operation and idling
Route deviations
Temperature and elevation where applicable

The same boat can produce different fuel-burn results on different days or different sections of the same trip.

Further context: Yamaha performance data, Mercury fuel-efficiency guidance, and Mercury trim guidance.

Finding Your Most Efficient Cruising Speed

Your most economical cruising speed is the practical operating point where the boat covers the greatest useful distance for the fuel consumed. It is not necessarily the slowest speed, and it is rarely useful to assume one RPM or one percentage of wide-open throttle for every boat.

The best way to find it is to compare speed and fuel-flow data across several normal operating RPM settings. When using statute miles, divide MPH by GPH to calculate MPG. When using knots, divide knots by GPH to estimate nautical miles per gallon.

Manufacturer performance bulletins can provide a useful starting point, but real fuel-flow data from your own boat is better because it reflects your hull, load, propeller and operating conditions.

Don't optimize for GPH alone. Optimize for distance per gallon at a speed that makes sense for the trip.

Mercury cruising-speed guidance and Yamaha fuel-management guidance.

Boat Fuel Planning Example
Example: 60-Nautical-Mile Round Trip
30 NM outbound
30 NM return
20-knot cruise
8 GPH cruise fuel burn
$4.50 per gallon
Outbound
30 NM ÷ 20 kn = 1.5 hours
1.5 hours × 8 GPH = 12 gallons
Return
30 NM ÷ 20 kn = 1.5 hours
1.5 hours × 8 GPH = 12 gallons

Expected trip consumption

12 + 12 = 24 gallons

Estimated fuel cost

24 × $4.50 = $108

In this simplified example, applying the U.S. Coast Guard's One-Third Rule would allocate approximately 12 gallons outbound, 12 gallons for the return and another 12 gallons as reserve — 36 usable gallons at departure. Real trips may require more because outbound and return conditions are rarely identical.

How Much Fuel Reserve Should You Carry?

The U.S. Coast Guard's A Boater's Guide to the Federal Requirements for Recreational Boats recommends practicing the One-Third Rule:

One-third of the fuel to go out
One-third to get back
One-third held in reserve

Treat the rule as a conservative fuel-management practice, not as a guarantee that a particular trip is safe. Wind, current, sea state, detours, no-wake zones and unexpected delays can increase actual consumption.

Use the Reserve Method control in the calculator above to apply the One-Third Rule or a percentage-based planning margin. Review the official U.S. Coast Guard boating guide for the One-Third Rule.

WHY FUEL PLANNING MATTERS
Safety First

Running out of fuel isn’t an option. Plan ahead and stay in control.

Weather Changes Everything

Wind, current, and sea state can significantly impact fuel burn.

Plan With Reserve

Build in reserve so you have options when conditions or plans change.

How Much Fuel Does a Boat Use Per Hour?

Boat fuel use is usually measured in gallons per hour, or GPH. There is no single GPH number that applies to every boat of a certain length or horsepower. Fuel burn changes with engine RPM and load, the hull, boat weight, propeller, trim, weather, current, sea state and other operating conditions.

The best number to use for trip planning is your boat's actual fuel burn at the speed you expect to cruise. If your engine display or fuel-flow system provides real-time GPH, use that value. Manufacturer performance tests for your specific boat and engine combination are the next-best reference.

Fuel burn can rise much faster than speed

One manufacturer test example: Yamaha tested a 23-foot Sportsman Open 232 with a single 300-hp F300 outboard. At 3,500 RPM the boat ran 27.2 mph while burning 8.3 GPH, or 3.28 MPG. At 5,800 RPM it ran 48.4 mph while burning 26.4 GPH, or 1.83 MPG.

In that test, speed increased about 78%, while hourly fuel consumption increased about 218%. That is why wide-open-throttle fuel burn should not be used as a substitute for actual cruising fuel burn.

Yamaha test data. This is one manufacturer test example, not a prediction for other boats.

These manufacturer performance tests show how fuel burn and fuel economy vary among specific boat and engine combinations at specific test RPM settings.

GPH vs. MPG: What the Numbers Mean
GPH — Gallons Per Hour

GPH tells you how quickly the engines are consuming fuel. If your boat burns 8 GPH for three hours, the trip consumes about 24 gallons before reserve or other adjustments.

Fuel Used = Running Hours × GPH
MPG — Miles Per Gallon

MPG measures how far the boat travels for each gallon burned. A higher GPH does not automatically mean worse fuel economy if the boat is also traveling substantially faster.

MPG = Speed in MPH ÷ GPH
Nautical Miles Per Gallon

When working in knots and nautical miles, the same idea can be expressed as nautical miles per gallon.

NM per Gallon = Speed in Knots ÷ GPH

For trip planning, GPH tells you the burn rate while distance-per-gallon measurements help identify the more economical cruising point.

Why Boat Fuel Consumption Changes With Speed

Boat fuel consumption does not increase in a simple one-to-one relationship with speed. As speed and engine load change, the hull's resistance through the water, running attitude and propulsion efficiency also change.

On a planing boat, efficiency can change significantly as the boat transitions onto plane and then continues toward higher RPM. More throttle normally increases gallons per hour, but the most useful efficiency measurement is how much distance the boat travels for each gallon consumed.

This is why the lowest GPH is not automatically the best cruising speed. Idling may burn very little fuel per hour but cover very little distance. At the other extreme, high RPM can dramatically increase GPH without providing a proportional increase in speed.

How to Find Your Boat's Actual GPH
Use onboard fuel-flow data

If your engine display, multifunction display or fuel-management system reports real-time GPH, use that data while operating at your normal cruising speed.

Yamaha states that its engine-management systems can continuously calculate fuel consumption and display information that lets operators evaluate fuel economy while underway.

Find a manufacturer performance bulletin

Search for a performance test matching your boat model, engine, horsepower and engine count. These reports commonly show RPM, speed, GPH and MPG at multiple throttle settings.

Yamaha Performance Bulletins

Compare with your own operating history

Fuel added, engine hours and trip records can help establish a real-world baseline when the operating profile is reasonably consistent.

One mixed-use tank does not automatically produce an accurate cruising GPH number.

Use a conservative estimate when necessary

If measured or manufacturer data is unavailable, use a conservative planning value and maintain additional reserve until you have enough real-world data to refine it.

Once you know your expected cruise GPH, enter it in the FloatPlanWizard calculator above along with distance, speed and reserve assumptions.

Boat & Load
Passengers

Overall operating weight

More weight generally requires more power to achieve and maintain a given operating condition.

Hull condition and drag affect how much power is required to move the boat through the water.

Engine, Propeller & Trim

Trim tabs where applicable
Engine condition

Propeller setup and trim affect the boat's running attitude and how efficiently engine power is converted into forward motion.

Conditions & Route
Wind

Temperature and elevation where applicable

The same boat can produce different fuel-burn results on different days or different sections of the same trip.

Further context: Yamaha performance data, Mercury fuel-efficiency guidance, and Mercury trim guidance.

Finding Your Most Efficient Cruising Speed

Your most economical cruising speed is the practical operating point where the boat covers the greatest useful distance for the fuel consumed. It is not necessarily the slowest speed, and it is rarely useful to assume one RPM or one percentage of wide-open throttle for every boat.

The best way to find it is to compare speed and fuel-flow data across several normal operating RPM settings. When using statute miles, divide MPH by GPH to calculate MPG. When using knots, divide knots by GPH to estimate nautical miles per gallon.

Manufacturer performance bulletins can provide a useful starting point, but real fuel-flow data from your own boat is better because it reflects your hull, load, propeller and operating conditions.

Don't optimize for GPH alone. Optimize for distance per gallon at a speed that makes sense for the trip.

Mercury cruising-speed guidance and Yamaha fuel-management guidance.

In this simplified example, applying the U.S. Coast Guard's One-Third Rule would allocate approximately 12 gallons outbound, 12 gallons for the return and another 12 gallons as reserve — 36 usable gallons at departure. Real trips may require more because outbound and return conditions are rarely identical.

How Much Fuel Reserve Should You Carry?

The U.S. Coast Guard's A Boater's Guide to the Federal Requirements for Recreational Boats recommends practicing the One-Third Rule:

One-third of the fuel to go out
One-third to get back
One-third held in reserve

Treat the rule as a conservative fuel-management practice, not as a guarantee that a particular trip is safe. Wind, current, sea state, detours, no-wake zones and unexpected delays can increase actual consumption.

Use the Reserve Method control in the calculator above to apply the One-Third Rule or a percentage-based planning margin. Review the official U.S. Coast Guard boating guide for the One-Third Rule.

mainText:
FloatPlanWizard
›
Great Loop Trip Planning

GREAT LOOP PLANNING GUIDE

Great Loop Trip Planning: How to Plan Locks, Bridges, Fuel and Daily Routes

Build a Great Loop route in FloatPlanWizard, review each leg, correct its drawn path and mileage, and turn the estimates into a realistic cruising day. Follow the current planning tools from saved waypoints through bridge and lock research, fuel checks and the Float Plan, then apply the workflow to a Chicago-to-Starved Rock corridor example.

Use reference pages to prepare; check conditions before departure.

This is a planning workflow, not a navigation route or a current operating notice. Confirm conditions, access and operating information for your selected route before relying on the plan.

In this guide
Plan one realistic leg
Prepare boat and waypoints
Generate the starting route
Inspect each leg
Correct leg mileage
Adjust or reuse the route
Review bridge constraints
Account for locks and delays
Check fuel with corrected NM
Build a realistic schedule
Choose a practical endpoint
Chicago / Illinois walkthrough
Prepare and share the Float Plan
Check the finished plan
Turn research into a plan
Plan the Great Loop one realistic leg at a time

A Great Loop route gives the trip direction; a daily leg gives the crew a workable plan. Start with where you intend to leave, the water you expect to travel, and a stopping point you can reconsider. Distance, bridges, locks, fuel and daylight belong in the same decision.

You can open FPW's Trip Planner workspace to continue to the FPW Route Generator once your Getting Started checklist is complete. Build a route from saved waypoints, inspect the legs, correct the drawn path where needed, and review the resulting distance, timing and fuel estimates. The finished route then supports a Float Plan for the trip you actually intend to run.

The workflow: prepare the boat and waypoints; build the route; review each leg; adjust its geometry; check bridges, locks, time and fuel; choose a realistic daily endpoint; save the route; then review and share the Float Plan.

Treat the generated result as the start of captain review. FPW organizes your planning; the captain still validates the navigable path with current charts, Notices to Mariners, official navigation information and judgment.

Start with the boat FPW is actually planning for

In the dashboard, complete Getting Started before creating a route: save a vessel, a shore contact with name, phone and email, an operator, and at least two waypoints. Add passengers when others will be aboard. Use the Waypoints panel to save the start and intended destination, checking each name, latitude and longitude. Two waypoints provide the endpoints of one leg; a return journey needs its own leg.

Know the boat's air draft in its intended configuration, draft under the expected load, usable fuel, normal cruise performance and the crew's realistic travel-day limit. Air draft and draft are checks you make against route constraints; the Route Generator does not certify bridge clearance or water depth.

Select the correct Vessel in the Route Generator, then review its planning inputs. Do not accept a speed or burn figure just because a field is populated.

Most Efficient Speed (kn) and GPH @ Efficient describe the cruising combination you expect to use.
Max Speed (kn) and GPH @ max speed support the faster-speed and relaxed-pace estimates. Review the displayed Adjusted Speed after choosing Pace.
Idle Burn (GPH) and Idle Hours (total) let you enter an explicit allowance for time with the engine idling.
Weather Factor (%) is a planning allowance. It is not confirmation of the conditions you will encounter.
Reserve Method and Underway Hrs / Day set fuel-reserve assumptions and the timeline's daily planning budget.

Use usable fuel rather than nominal tank size when checking range in the Boat Fuel Calculator. Measure and confirm your own boat's limits instead of adopting another captain's figures.

Generate your starting Great Loop route

The current member workflow is My Routes & Waypoint Builder. You select saved waypoints to define the route; this screen does not offer an automatic Great Loop itinerary or a visible route-template picker.

On the dashboard, choose + Create Route. Enter a descriptive Route Name. The guided tour can help identify the controls.
In Create Route, enter the route name and choose Create. This creates the My Route you will build; it does not send a Float Plan.
Choose your departure waypoint under Route Start Waypoint, then choose Set Start.
Under Add Leg by Waypoint, select the next intended waypoint and choose Add Leg. Repeat for additional legs. The next destination extends the sequence from the previous endpoint.
Choose Load to populate Route Summary and Legs and the Cruise Timeline. Confirm the vessel, speed, fuel and daily-hours inputs.
Review and adjust the result before using Save Route. Saving a route and sending a Float Plan are separate actions.
Create or select a My Route, set its start, and add each next waypoint before choosing Load. This local practice route demonstrates the controls; it is not a Great Loop itinerary. Select the image for a larger view.

A waypoint leg may begin with a straight-line distance and no saved navigable geometry. A line between two coordinates does not establish a usable channel. Use the leg review and geometry steps below before treating that distance as a cruising estimate.

Review the route one leg at a time

Under Cruise Timeline, review each leg's start and destination, Locks count, effective NM and Edit Route control. The summary above provides Total Distance, Total Travel Hours, Estimated Fuel and Adjusted Speed. These are estimates based on the route and inputs currently loaded.

Read the leg endpoints and NM, then choose Edit Route when the path needs review. The practice values demonstrate the interface, not a recommended distance or cruising schedule. Select the image for a larger view.
Does the path follow the waterway and approach you intend to use? Check more than the endpoint names.
Does the leg's distance reflect that path, including approaches and deliberate detours?
Which bridges and locks actually lie on this leg? A zero lock count on a waypoint-only leg does not establish that no locks are present.
At the selected pace, does the running time leave room for waiting, maneuvering, conditions and a suitable stopping point?

The timeline can allocate a long leg across planning days. A day boundary is a time-budget result; it is not a verified marina, anchorage or safe place to stop. Review the complete leg and the practical stopping options yourself.

Generated mileage is a starting point — correct the path when necessary

FPW's current mileage override is a geometry edit. There is no numeric “actual mileage” box in this workflow. You draw or edit the expected path and FPW calculates Computed NM from that line. This is planned distance, not a measurement of a voyage already traveled.

Use this when a direct line misses the navigable channel, an approach is longer than the initial estimate, or your intended path changes because of a constraint. The line must reflect a path you have independently checked; adding points to a map does not validate safe passage.

Choose Edit Route beside the leg in Cruise Timeline or in the My Route's Leg Sequence. The Leg Geometry panel opens.
Check the leg title, its source and Computed NM. If there is no saved geometry, the panel says to draw a polyline.
Use the map's Draw a polyline control to trace the expected path. Click successive points and finish the line. For an existing drawn line, use Edit layers and finish that map edit. Check the start, end and intermediate points.
Review the recalculated Computed NM, then choose Save Overrides. Finishing the map drawing alone is not the same as saving the override.
Close the map panel and inspect the leg's updated NM and Override indication. Choose Load for the selected My Route to review its current total, timeline and fuel estimate again before saving the route.
Use the drawing controls to describe the reviewed path, check Computed NM, and save the override. This example shows a saved user override for Chicago to Joliet; its map and values are not navigation instructions. Select the image for a larger view.

What is saved: FPW stores the drawn geometry and its calculated mileage as your override. The My Route's base distance remains separate. The visible leg shows the effective distance; it does not display the original and overridden mileages side by side. Note the original value before editing if you want to compare them.

What changes: the effective leg distance and route total change. When the route is reloaded or its estimates are rebuilt, the adjusted distance feeds the timing and Route Generator fuel calculations. A longer expected path can therefore change the planning hours, fuel requirement and daily allocation.

What to check separately: an existing generated route's geometry save can update NM before its previous timeline and fuel display refresh. Save the edited route and review the refreshed estimates; do not rely on an unchanged time or fuel card immediately after a map save. This does not automatically revise an already-created Float Plan's return time or the separate public Fuel Calculator.

Change or remove an override: reopen Edit Route, revise the line and save again. Revert to Default removes the applicable saved override and reloads the available default; verify the resulting NM. Clear Draw clears the working drawing; saving that cleared state also removes the override. Do not treat Clear Draw as a private sketch reset once you save it. On a previously generated route, the default can be its saved base distance, so check the result rather than assuming it restores an earlier estimate. Revert to Default on an existing generated route also clears any saved segment-wide override, which can affect other routes using that saved segment geometry.

Adjust the route when reality requires it

Decide whether you are changing the path between the same endpoints or the endpoints of the day's route. A geometry override addresses the first. It does not change the leg's destination, reorder the route or discover the bridges and locks crossed by the new line.

For a different endpoint, save the needed waypoint on the dashboard and return to My Routes & Waypoint Builder. Add Leg extends the current route. To replace the final destination, use Remove on the final leg, select the new destination, then choose Add Leg. Removing an intermediate leg reconnects the following leg and clears that following leg's saved geometry override. Review its new endpoints and redraw the path where needed. Check every adjacent start and destination before choosing Load.

This is useful when a bridge constraint changes an approach, a lock transit makes the day too long, weather suggests a shorter run, or fuel margin calls for a different stopping decision. Change the proposed route to match the plan you can defend, then check distance, references, time and fuel again.

Reuse deliberately: select a saved My Route to load it again. Geometry overrides are saved with their route context; do not assume one edit updates every other route using similar waters. After changing the leg sequence or regenerating a saved route, reopen each edited leg and verify that its geometry and mileage still belong to the correct endpoints. Reset is not a general undo of changes already saved.

Plan these changes before departure. An active trip has additional controls and restrictions; this tutorial does not promise that rebuilding an active route will safely replace its live itinerary.

Connect Great Loop bridge research to the route you drew
Start with the proposed route and open the Great Loop Bridges references. Identify the entries relevant to the waterways and approach you intend to use.
Compare your boat's air draft with the applicable information. Distinguish fixed structures from opening bridges and closed clearance from open clearance. Confirm current conditions and operating information before depending on passage.
If the approach changes, decide whether to edit a leg's geometry or rebuild the waypoint sequence. A drawn override does not perform an automatic clearance check.
Load the changed route and review mileage, timing and fuel again. An approach change can affect more than the bridge crossing itself.

For the Chicago-area example, use the Illinois / Chicago bridge references and the Chicago River approach reference. The latter provides context for evaluating downtown Chicago and Cal-Sag alternatives. Use it to organize the comparison; it does not select a suitable approach for your vessel.

Running time is only part of a lock day

A realistic day may include underway time, lock approach and maneuvering, waiting, lock passage, bridge timing, fuel or rest stops, and weather margin. Distance divided by speed covers only part of that day.

Open the Great Loop Locks library while reviewing the leg. Identify the facilities relevant to the selected path and use their individual pages as planning references. Confirm actual access and operating information separately; stored reference information is not a live queue or operating notice.

Where a route leg has mapped lock information, its expanded Lock Navigation Details can show Best, Typical and Worst waiting estimates and notes. These are stored planning assumptions, not live waiting times. Waypoint-only legs may have no canonical lock mapping; absence of details does not mean there is no lock to research.

For the My Route workflow taught here, do not assume lock delays are automatically added to the timeline. A lock count or details panel is not proof that waiting and lock passage have been included. There is no per-lock delay entry in this screen.

Estimate extra time separately from running time. For expected engine-idling time, enter an allowance in Idle Hours (total) and confirm Idle Burn (GPH). That affects the summary hours and idle-fuel estimate; it does not automatically move the timeline's daily boundaries. Keep non-idling waits, bridge timing, shore stops and additional margin in your own schedule as well. Count each allowance once.

Use the corrected mileage to check fuel
Finish reviewing the path and reload the route. Read the effective leg NM and Total Distance. If you are checking one cruising day, use the distance you actually intend to cover that day rather than the entire multi-day route.
Open the Boat Fuel Calculator and manually enter that value in Total Distance (NM). Route Generator distances do not automatically transfer to this public calculator.
Enter your Most Efficient Speed (kn), GPH @ Efficient, Max Speed (kn) and applicable Fuel Burn @ Max (GPH). Choose Pace and review the Weather Factor (%) assumption.
Enter expected Idle Hours and Idle Burn (GPH) where appropriate. Use Usable Fuel Capacity and select your Reserve Method; do not substitute nominal tank size for fuel you can actually use.
Review estimated fuel and range against usable fuel and the reserve you intend to preserve. Confirm practical refueling arrangements separately. If margin is uncomfortable, shorten or revise the leg and repeat the calculation.

The Route Generator also provides its own fuel estimate using the loaded route and its inputs. The public calculator is a separate manual check, not a synchronized view of that route. Match distance, pace, burn, weather and idle assumptions deliberately, and update both tools after a material change.

Neither result guarantees consumption or fuel availability. A comfortable estimate is useful only if the chosen path, boat performance and allowances are realistic.

Turn generated mileage into a realistic day's schedule

Distance alone is not the schedule. FPW uses effective leg mileage, the selected pace and speed inputs, and weather adjustments to estimate running time. The timeline uses the daily-hours budget to group travel into planning days. It does not establish a guaranteed arrival clock time or confirm an overnight stop.

Finalize the leg geometry and choose Load to review the current NM. Verify the displayed distance after every material route change.
Confirm the selected Vessel, speed inputs and Pace. Review Adjusted Speed and Total Travel Hours. The weather allowance can affect modeled speed; it does not replace checking the forecast.
Set Underway Hrs / Day to a realistic travel budget. Review the resulting allocation, particularly any leg split across planning days.
Add your researched lock and bridge allowances, fuel/rest stops and margin to the day's running estimate. Treat Idle Hours as a summary allowance, not an automatic appointment scheduler.
Compare the realistic total with your departure window, daylight and intended arrival. If the day is too ambitious, change the waypoint endpoint or shorten the planned run and load it again.
When preparing the Float Plan, review its departure and Return Date & Time in the selected timezone. Set a realistic return value; an earlier geometry or idle-time edit is not confirmation that the Float Plan's time has changed.

The generated estimate helps compare choices. Your captain-adjusted schedule adds the constraints that the model does not know. Keep those assumptions available when you review the route and explain the plan to your shore contact.

Choose the daily stopping point after reviewing the estimates

Use the combined distance, running time, delays and fuel requirement to decide where the day should end. A timeline split is not a recommendation to stop at that exact point. Check whether a marina, anchorage, mooring or other stopping area is suitable, accessible and available for your boat.

Save an appropriate waypoint for the endpoint you have researched and use it when building the day's route. If the current leg goes farther than the day can support, revise the waypoint sequence and review the changed geometry and NM. FPW does not confirm marina availability or make stopping arrangements for you.

Identify an earlier suitable option before departure. When a meaningful delay changes remaining time, daylight or fuel margin, reconsider the endpoint while alternatives remain available. Communicate material route or timing changes to your shore contact.

Worked example: Building a Chicago-area Loop leg in FPW

Use Chicago toward the Starved Rock corridor to practice the workflow. This is a planning/reference example, not a guaranteed lock sequence or prescribed itinerary. It does not assume the corridor is one day's run. Choose the actual start, approach and daily endpoint for your boat and conditions. The practice screenshots above illustrate the controls only; they do not depict this corridor.

Build the starting route. Save the waypoints for the departure and intended endpoint you are evaluating. Choose + Create Route, name the My Route, choose Set Start, add the next waypoint with Add Leg, and choose Load. Do not assume the initial line follows the waterway.
Review Chicago bridge constraints. Use the Illinois / Chicago references to compare the selected approach with your boat's air draft. Determine which path needs further checking before accepting the route.
Review potentially relevant lock references. The Chicago / Illinois Waterway references help organize that research. The following list is unordered and does not establish a travel sequence:
Brandon Road Lock
Dresden Island Lock
Lockport Lock
Marseilles Lock
Starved Rock Lock
Thomas J. O'Brien Lock
Relevance depends on the approach and endpoints. FPW also provides a Chicago Harbor Lock reference for optional downtown routing. Establish the actual facilities and order on your selected route independently.
Inspect every leg's mileage. Compare its endpoints and effective NM with the navigable path you intend to run. Review the approach, not just the corridor's place names.
Correct the expected path where needed. Choose Edit Route, draw or edit the reviewed geometry, inspect Computed NM and choose Save Overrides. This replaces the distance used for that leg with the distance calculated from your saved line; it is not a numeric mileage-entry field.
Reevaluate running time. Load the My Route again. Confirm speed, pace, daily hours and the refreshed estimate. Do not carry forward the first distance or timing figure after changing the path.
Account for locks and other delay. Use the selected lock references and current operating information to build your own allowance. The custom My Route timeline does not automatically include those lock delays. Enter expected idle time for the fuel/summary calculation and review the full schedule separately.
Check fuel. Enter the corrected daily distance manually in the Boat Fuel Calculator. Apply the boat's realistic performance, idle allowance and reserve. Revise the leg if the margin is inadequate.
Decide where the day should end. Evaluate a suitable endpoint against realistic time, fuel and daylight. If necessary, revise the waypoint sequence and repeat the review before saving the route and preparing the Float Plan.

The goal is to turn the initial route into the route you actually intend to run. A useful result is a reviewed plan with room to adapt, not a promised arrival at Starved Rock.

Turn the finished route into the trip you'll actually run

After reviewing the route and choosing Save Route, return to the dashboard's Routes list. The Activate Route action prepares a draft Float Plan and opens its editor. Despite that action's name, this step alone does not send the plan or start monitoring. An existing draft can be reopened with Complete Float Plan.

Work through the Float Plan editor: confirm the vessel and operator, passengers where applicable, route details, departure, return date/time and timezone. Review the itinerary instead of assuming that every earlier planning change has already updated the draft. Select the intended shore contact and check the final review.

Save Float Plan saves the draft without sending. The review screen presents separate send choices: Basic Save & Send emails a PDF copy to one selected contact and leaves the plan as a draft; Premium Save & Send uses the operational sharing path when the account qualifies. Follow the explanation shown for the action you choose rather than treating these choices as equivalent.

Arrange a shore contact who agrees to receive and understand the trip details. Share the reviewed plan before departure, confirm expectations for check-ins and changes, and review how a Float Plan helps your shore contact. Saving or generating a route alone does not notify anyone.

For a later voyage, start from the saved route and review the new trip's details and schedule. Do not reuse an old shared plan as evidence that someone has received the current plan.

Before accepting tomorrow's Great Loop leg

Review the tools and decisions together before departure:

Boat air draft, draft, loading and usable fuel reviewed
Saved waypoints checked; intended route built and loaded in FPW
Every leg's endpoints, navigable path and generated NM reviewed
Geometry overrides saved where needed; resulting leg and route NM checked
Bridge constraints and relevant lock references reviewed for the selected path
Vessel, speed inputs and Pace confirmed
Fresh timing estimate and Underway Hrs / Day reviewed
Lock/bridge waits, idle time, stops and margin considered without double-counting
Corrected daily NM entered manually in the Fuel Calculator
Fuel requirement checked and intended reserve preserved
Daily endpoint and earlier alternative researched for suitability and availability
Weather and current operating information checked
Changed routes reloaded; edited legs and totals checked again
Float Plan itinerary, departure, return time and timezone reviewed
Shore contact identified; final Float Plan ready to share before departure

Your boating budget

What would an actual trip cost?

Browser saving stays on this device, is not an account backup, may disappear when browser data is cleared, and expires after 180 days. Nothing is saved until you choose Save.

Anyone with a share link can view its figures. The link is not private and cannot be revoked. Scenario labels are omitted.

What a boat costs beyond the loan payment

A boat payment is only one part of the budget. Add fuel, storage, insurance, routine maintenance, registration and recurring taxes, seasonal services, utilities, towing and trailer costs. Keep purchase taxes and fees separate from annual bills. Money saved for future repairs is a funding choice, not an expense or a prediction that repairs will cost that amount.

Monthly figures spread annual and seasonal costs across 12 months; actual bill timing varies. A blank field means unknown. Enter zero only when zero is your assumption; exclude a category when you deliberately leave it out. Exclusions remain visible with the estimate.

How to estimate your operating costs

Use insurer and marina quotes, service records and your own usage estimates. Storage can include a year-round slip and seasonal land storage; review overlapping contracts. A marina's billable length can differ from the boat's physical length. Seasonal boating does not automatically reduce insurance, loan payments or annual storage contracts.

Enter annual fuel dollars, or annual boat running hours multiplied by total GPH for all propulsion engines and price per US gallon. Two engines using 8 GPH each means 16 total GPH. Generator use is separate. Unburned trip reserve fuel is not an annual consumption expense.

Need to check the fuel cost for a specific trip? Use the Boat Fuel Calculator.

Use measured consumption or appropriate performance data. Read how to find your boat's actual GPH, then check trip fuel costs. FPW does not look up a model's GPH from its name, length or horsepower.

Keep routine engine services separate from seasonal work and immediate repairs. Electric or mixed-propulsion owners can enter annual energy spending in other operating costs and explicitly exclude liquid fuel.

New versus used boats and first-year preparation

A used boat can require a survey, inspection haul-out, engine inspection and catch-up work before normal use. Review delivery, immediate repairs, batteries, electronics, safety equipment, bottom work and a trailer. Some costs arise before closing; others arrive later in the first year. The upfront planning cash figure conservatively includes them all.

Review sails and rigging for a sailboat; bottom work, haul-out and marina utilities for a boat kept in water; and trailer upkeep, towing and launch fees for a trailered boat. Multiple engines can mean multiple service bills. The checklist changes with the boat profile, but entered costs never receive hidden multipliers. An entered repair reserve does not establish mechanical condition or seaworthiness.

How loan length changes payment and interest

For a fixed principal and positive interest rate, a longer term generally lowers each monthly payment while increasing lifetime interest. Compare the payment and interest together. Actual lender terms, rates and vessel eligibility may differ.

Use the loan's contract interest rate for this amortization estimate. APR incorporates additional borrowing charges; this tool does not calculate a regulatory APR. See the CFPB explanation of interest rate and APR. No live rates or lender approval are supplied.

Start with your monthly budget and available cash

The budget direction finds the highest boat price within both your monthly limit and your available upfront cash. It holds operating expenses, preparation and repair savings fixed. Percentage down payments and percentage purchase tax change with the candidate price; fixed dollar inputs stay fixed.

The budget result holds your operating assumptions fixed. A different boat may have different costs. It is not a personal financial recommendation or a loan approval. Unknown expenses must be reviewed before the solver can provide a complete result.

Methodology and exclusions

Loan principal equals boat price minus down payment plus financed purchase tax and fees. Cash for purchase equals down payment plus cash-paid purchase tax and fees. Preparation is counted once. Monthly boating budget equals the loan payment plus one twelfth of annual operating expenses and annual repair savings.

First-year spending adds purchase cash, preparation, the first 12 scheduled loan payments and annual operations. The first-year funding target adds initial and annual repair savings. A horizon's optional resale-adjusted cost equals cash spent plus remaining loan balance plus selling costs minus assumed resale. Do not add depreciation or the whole purchase price again.

Entered monetary values and percentage-derived charges use cents with half-up rounding; amortization retains full precision until display. BOATING SAFETY GUIDE

When Something Goes Wrong on the Water

A practical, step-by-step guide to common boating emergencies for everyday recreational boaters.

Most boating problems do not begin as dramatic emergencies. An engine stops. The bilge pump runs longer than usual. A passenger slips. The wind rises faster than expected. What happens next often depends on whether the operator recognizes the danger, protects the people aboard, controls what can be controlled, and asks for help before the situation becomes critical.

This guide explains the first actions to take during common problems on recreational powerboats, pontoons, fishing boats, bowriders, deck boats, and small cruisers. Read it before you need it, review the sections that apply to your boat, and keep the printable quick-reference card where the operator and passengers can reach it.

Reviewed August 22, 2026

Start with the first 60 seconds
Print this guide

IMMEDIATE DANGER

If anyone is in immediate danger

Put on life jackets, address the immediate threat, and call for help without delay. Use VHF Channel 16 and make a Mayday call when a person or vessel is threatened by grave and imminent danger and needs immediate assistance. If VHF is unavailable, call 911 and be ready to give your location, boat description, number of people aboard, and the nature of the emergency.

This guide supplements—not replaces—a boating-safety course, the Navigation Rules, local law, your boat and engine manuals, first-aid training, or instructions from emergency responders.

In 2024, the U.S. Coast Guard verified 3,887 recreational boating incidents involving 556 deaths and 2,170 injuries. Collisions, groundings, swamping, and falls overboard were among the most consequential events. Where the cause of death was known, 76 percent of fatal victims drowned; where life-jacket use was known, 87 percent of those drowning victims were not wearing one.

The lesson is not that every outing is dangerous. It is that ordinary problems deserve an organized response—and that life jackets, a reliable position, early communication, and practiced emergency equipment matter.

FIRST RESPONSE

The first 60 seconds of a boating emergency

When something goes wrong, use P.A.C.E.: People, Assess, Control, Emergency call. P.A.C.E. is a FloatPlanWizard memory aid created for this guide; it is not an official Coast Guard acronym.

Illustrative sequence; equipment and safe actions depend on the vessel and emergency.

P

Protect and account for people
Account for everyone aboard. If someone is missing, treat it as a person-overboard emergency immediately.
Have everyone put on a properly fitted life jacket. A life jacket stored under gear cannot help during a sudden fall, collision, or capsize.
Move passengers away from fuel, smoke, fire, machinery, spinning propellers, damaged electrical equipment, open hatches, and lines under load.
Assign short, specific jobs when capable people are available: “Watch the person in the water,” “Get our position,” “Bring the life jackets,” or “Make the radio call.”

A

Assess what can hurt you next
Is anyone injured, missing, trapped, or in the water?
Is the boat burning, flooding, losing stability, or unable to maneuver?
Are you drifting toward rocks, surf, shoal water, a dam, a bridge, another boat, or a busy channel?
Is weather, darkness, current, or distance from help shrinking your safety margin?

Do not let troubleshooting distract you from a growing external danger. A minor engine problem can become an emergency if the boat is drifting into an inlet, shipping channel, surf line, or lee shore.

C

Control what you safely can

The correct action depends on the problem. You may need to reduce speed, shift to neutral, shut down the engine, maintain just enough steerage to clear traffic, anchor, start bilge pumps, close a known seacock, or prepare a throwable flotation device. Do not perform a memorized action blindly.

Record your position as early as possible. Use latitude and longitude from a GPS/chartplotter or identify a reliable landmark, navigation aid, channel marker, bridge, marina, or shoreline feature. Note the direction of drift and whether the situation is stable, improving, or worsening.

E

Make the emergency call early

Call before the boat loses electrical power, communications, buoyancy, daylight, or distance from danger. If crew is available, one person can communicate while another handles the immediate physical response.

Do not wait to complete every P.A.C.E. step before calling. A person overboard, uncontrolled fire or flooding, serious injury, collision risk, or other immediate danger requires action and communication at the same time when possible.

Prepare the information someone ashore may need

Create and share a float plan with your route, people, boat, contacts, timing, and safety details.

Create a Float Plan
→

COMMUNICATION

What kind of help do you need?
Mayday: grave and imminent danger

Use Mayday when a person or boat faces grave and imminent danger and needs immediate assistance. Examples can include:

A person missing in the water
Uncontrolled flooding or sinking
A fire that is not immediately controlled
A life-threatening injury or medical emergency
A collision with serious injuries or major damage
A disabled boat drifting into surf, rocks, a dam, heavy traffic, or another immediate hazard

If you are unsure whether the danger is grave and imminent, describe the facts clearly to the Coast Guard or local authority. Do not minimize a deteriorating situation because you are embarrassed or hope to fix it yourself.

Pan-Pan: urgent but not yet grave and imminent

The urgency signal is pronounced “pahn-pahn.” It is used when the safety of a boat or person is in jeopardy but the situation has not reached Mayday-level distress. Examples could include a controllable leak, a serious mechanical problem in a hazardous area, or a disabled boat drifting toward a channel while there is still time to respond.

Conditions change. Escalate to Mayday if the danger becomes grave and imminent.

PAN-PAN, PAN-PAN, PAN-PAN
ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS — or the specific Coast Guard station being called
THIS IS [boat name repeated three times, then registration/call sign]
MY POSITION IS [latitude/longitude or clear location]
WE HAVE [urgent problem]
WE NEED [assistance/advice]
THERE ARE [number] PEOPLE ABOARD
[Drift, injuries, boat description, and other useful facts]
OVER

This is a practical plain-language template built around the FCC urgency signal and normal marine call content; local authorities may direct a different working channel or procedure. Keep the initial Channel 16 transmission brief and follow instructions.

Routine assistance

A stable boat with no injuries, no flooding or fire, safe weather, reliable communications, and no drift toward danger may need a commercial tow, fuel delivery, or mechanical help rather than an emergency response. Continue monitoring position, weather, battery power, and the condition of everyone aboard while assistance is coming.

VHF or cellphone?

Use a marine VHF radio as the primary on-water emergency tool when available. A VHF call can be heard by the Coast Guard and nearby boats, and a properly configured DSC radio can transmit a digital distress alert. A cellphone depends on shore-based coverage, reaches only the number called, and may not automatically give marine responders a useful position.

If VHF is unavailable, call 911. State that you are on a boat, give your location early, and stay available for instructions. Use every reliable means available when life is at risk.

VHF CHANNEL 16

How to make a Mayday call on VHF Channel 16

The U.S. Coast Guard Navigation Center (opens in a new tab) recommends the following information. Speak slowly and clearly:

Give position, danger, assistance needed, and people aboard. Keep the full Mayday script in HTML and on the printable card.

MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY
THIS IS [boat name repeated three times]
[Boat name and registration number or call sign]
MAYDAY [boat name]
MY POSITION IS [latitude/longitude or clear location]
WE ARE [nature of distress]
WE NEED [assistance required]
THERE ARE [number of adults and children] PEOPLE ABOARD
[Injuries, boat type/length/color, drift, and other useful information]
OVER

Stay near the radio when possible. Answer questions, follow instructions, and repeat the call at intervals if no one responds. Preserve battery power, but do not turn off the only radio responders are using to reach or locate you.

If the radio has DSC

A DSC distress button can send a formatted alert to equipped rescue stations and nearby DSC radios. For the alert to identify the boat and include its position, the radio must have a properly registered Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) and current GPS position data from an internal or connected receiver.

Know your radio before an emergency:

Register and program the MMSI correctly.
Confirm that current position data appears on the radio.
Teach another passenger how to lift the distress cover, press and hold the button as the radio requires, and make the follow-up voice call on Channel 16.
Never press the distress button for a radio check.
If activated accidentally, follow the radio manual and Coast Guard procedure to cancel the false alert immediately.

BOAT PROBLEMS

What to do if the boat engine dies or you lose propulsion

An engine failure may be an inconvenience in open, calm water and an immediate emergency near surf, rocks, a bridge, a dam, shoal water, or heavy traffic. Deal with the boat’s movement before diagnosing the engine.

Assess depth, bottom, traffic, wind, current, and sea room before anchoring or troubleshooting.
Do this first
Maintain a lookout and determine what the boat is drifting toward.
Put life jackets on everyone.
Record the position and observe drift direction.
If anchoring is appropriate, deploy the anchor from the bow before the boat reaches danger. Confirm adequate depth, scope, bottom conditions, swinging room, current, and traffic. Do not anchor in a channel unless it is necessary for immediate safety, and warn approaching traffic.
If anchoring is unsafe or impossible, make the appropriate urgency or distress call early and take the safest available action to avoid collision or grounding.
Then check the simple causes

Only after the boat is stable enough to troubleshoot, check items the operator can verify without opening fuel systems or exposing anyone to machinery:

Is the throttle/shift control fully in neutral?
Is the engine cut-off switch clip or wireless fob correctly engaged?
Are battery switches in the intended position?
Do instruments and electronics have power?
Are battery terminals visibly loose or badly corroded? Do not work on electrical connections if fuel vapor is present.
Is there fuel according to more than an unreliable gauge, and is the correct tank selected?
Is a portable fuel-tank vent open where the design requires it?
Is a fuel line visibly kinked or a primer bulb collapsed?
Has a breaker tripped or a clearly labeled engine fuse failed?
Is the propeller fouled or damaged? Inspect only with the engine shut down, the key removed or start controls disabled, and nobody able to start it. Do not enter the water to clear a propeller as a routine response.
Did an alarm, overheating indication, low oil-pressure warning, or reduced-power mode occur? Follow the engine manual; do not repeatedly restart an engine that may be overheating, starved of lubrication, or mechanically damaged.

Stop if the cause is not obvious and safely correctable. Repeated cranking can drain the starting battery and eliminate radio, pump, navigation-light, and electronics capacity.

Do not do this
Do not focus on the engine while the boat drifts into danger.
Do not anchor from the stern; waves or wake over a low transom can swamp a small boat.
Do not bypass safety switches, create sparks, open fuel fittings, or improvise wiring repairs around gasoline vapor.
Do not assume a cellphone call means nearby boats know you need help.
Do not accept an unsafe towline arrangement from an unprepared helper.
Call for help now if…
The boat is drifting toward traffic, rocks, surf, a dam, bridge, shoal, or lee shore.
Weather or visibility is deteriorating.
Anchoring is not possible or the anchor is dragging.
Anyone is injured, ill, in the water, or unable to remain safe aboard.
The boat is also taking on water, losing electrical power, or becoming unstable.
You cannot give a reliable position or expect communications to fail.
After you are safe

Cancel or update any assistance request if the engine restarts. Return at conservative speed, monitor alarms and gauges, and have the cause inspected before relying on the boat again.

For pre-departure planning, calculate a safer fuel reserve.

BOAT PROBLEMS

What to do if steering, throttle, or electrical controls fail

Loss of steering or throttle can remove control faster than an engine shutdown. The first priority is preventing a collision—not preserving the trip.

Do this first
Reduce power carefully if throttle control remains available.
Shift to neutral or shut down propulsion when that is the safest way to prevent injury or collision.
Warn passengers, account for everyone, and put on life jackets.
Sound the horn and make a safety or urgency call if other traffic may not understand your movement.
Use a second engine, auxiliary steering, emergency tiller, or other manufacturer-provided system only if the operator knows how it works and can deploy it safely.
Anchor when appropriate and before the boat reaches danger.

Electrical failure may also disable navigation lights, pumps, radios, engine controls, trim systems, and electronic steering. Preserve any remaining battery-powered communications. A charged handheld VHF, waterproof flashlight, manual pump, paper chart, and compass can keep one failure from becoming several.

Limited safe checks
Confirm battery-switch position and visible voltage indications.
Check clearly labeled main breakers and fuses once; a breaker that trips again is evidence of a fault, not an invitation to keep resetting it.
Look and smell for overheating wiring, smoke, melting insulation, or fuel vapor.
Check accessible steering-linkage or hydraulic-fluid indications only as described in the boat manual.
Do not do this
Do not reach into moving steering, belt, pulley, or linkage components.
Do not repeatedly reset a breaker or replace a fuse with a higher rating.
Do not make improvised electrical connections around gasoline fumes.
Do not continue at speed with intermittent steering or throttle response.
Call for help now if…

You cannot reliably control course or speed, the boat is in traffic or confined water, weather is worsening, navigation lights are unavailable near darkness, pumps or communications are affected, or a burning smell/smoke suggests an electrical fire.

BOAT PROBLEMS

What to do if the boat is taking on water

Treat unexplained water entry seriously. Bilge pumps buy time; they do not make an uncontrolled leak safe. The rate matters: compare whether the water level is rising, steady, or falling while pumps run.

Boat layouts differ. Check only accessible areas you understand, and never delay a distress call while water is rising.
Do this first
Put life jackets on everyone and make sure children and non-swimmers remain supervised.
Start all installed bilge pumps and use manual pumps or buckets if they can be used without delaying the distress call.
Give the position and make a Mayday call if water is rising rapidly, the source cannot be controlled, electrical power or stability is threatened, or sinking is possible.
Assign one person to monitor the water level and another to communicate if crew is available.
Keep people out of the bilge and away from batteries, exposed wiring, hot machinery, and contaminated water.
Look for a cause only when it is safe

Common sources include:

A missing or leaking drain plug
A failed hose, clamp, through-hull fitting, seacock, transducer, livewell, washdown, or raw-water connection
A damaged outdrive bellows, shaft seal, rudder port, or other underwater fitting
A cooling or exhaust-system hose that leaks while the engine is running
Hull damage after striking an object or running aground
Water coming over a low transom because of waves, wake, overloading, or too much weight aft
Rain, spray, or deck drains/scuppers that cannot clear water fast enough

If the operator can identify a known seacock feeding a failed hose, close it. Use a properly sized soft wooden plug or other purpose-made damage-control material on an accessible opening. A towel, cushion, or other soft material pressed against a damaged area may slow water temporarily, but do not depend on an improvised patch or put someone in a position where they can be trapped.

If water entry changes with the engine running, shut the engine down if doing so is safe and observe the result. A cooling or exhaust failure can pump substantial water into the boat. Balance that action against the need for steerage; tell responders exactly what is happening.

Reduce the flooding risk
Keep the bow oriented to waves when safe and controllable; avoid allowing following seas to board over a low transom.
Move people and portable weight away from the flooded or low side without creating instability elsewhere.
Do not open large compartments unnecessarily in rough water.
Prepare visual distress signals and a registered beacon if carried.
Bring essential communications and flotation together in case the boat must be abandoned, but remain aboard unless staying creates greater danger.
Do not do this
Do not wait for the bilge pump to “catch up” while the water level continues to rise.
Do not send someone overboard or under the boat to find a leak.
Do not work near a running engine, propeller shaft, belts, batteries, or submerged electrical equipment.
Do not intentionally beach the boat without considering people on the beach, surf, rocks, hull design, pollution, and responder instructions. In a life-threatening situation, follow the safest available option and tell responders what you intend to do.
Call for help now if…
Water is rising with all pumps operating.
The source cannot be found or reached safely.
The boat has struck something or grounded hard.
Batteries, engines, pumps, or steering are being submerged.
The boat is listing, settling lower, or becoming difficult to control.
Fire, fuel, sewage, or electrical hazards are present.
After you are safe

Do not place the boat back in service merely because the water was pumped out. Find and repair the cause, inspect affected electrical and mechanical systems, and report the incident when required.

BOAT PROBLEMS

What to do if you see smoke, smell gasoline, discover a fuel leak, or have a fire

Fuel vapor, smoke, and fire demand different reactions, but all can become life-threatening quickly on a boat. Warn everyone immediately and call early if the source is not identified and controlled.

Fire at a fuel dock can spread rapidly from the engine compartment to spilled fuel on the water. Stop fueling, alert everyone nearby, evacuate to a safe location and call emergency services—do not remain aboard to fight a spreading fuel fire.
Fuel-Dock Fires and Burning Fuel on the Water

Fueling may feel routine, but a fuel dock combines gasoline, vapors, electrical equipment, boats and people in a confined area. Even a small spill can spread across the water and underneath nearby boats or docks.

The water itself does not burn. A layer of fuel floating on the surface—and the vapor above it—can ignite and carry fire rapidly across the fueling area.

A lesson I never forgot

When I was about 10 years old, I was aboard my father’s 14-foot runabout while we stopped for fuel. A larger boat was fueling beside us. Although nothing appeared to be leaking at that moment, some fuel was already floating on the water.

A man aboard the other boat was smoking a cigar. He threw it into the water, apparently intending to put it out, and the fuel on the surface ignited almost instantly.

Everything happened very fast. My mother panicked and jumped into the water. Someone grabbed me and ran with me as quickly as possible to get away from the fire. Thankfully, my mother was unharmed and the fire was extinguished, but the situation could easily have ended very differently.

That experience stayed with me because every part of it was preventable. Smoking should never have been permitted near the fuel dock, spilled fuel should not have been present, and no passenger—especially a child—should have remained aboard during fueling.

Before fueling
Put all passengers ashore before fueling begins.
Secure the boat firmly to the dock.
Shut down engines, generators and other potential ignition sources.
Extinguish cigarettes, cigars and every open flame. If anyone begins smoking nearby, stop fueling immediately and alert the dock attendant.
Close ports, hatches and doors to keep gasoline vapors out of enclosed spaces.
Keep the fuel nozzle in contact with the fill opening and attend it continuously.
Fill slowly and never top off the tank.
Watch the fuel vent, deck and surrounding water for spills or a visible sheen.

After fueling, open the compartments, ventilate the boat and operate the blower for at least four minutes before starting a gasoline engine. Check carefully for fuel odors. Reboard passengers only after the engine has been started safely. These precautions follow BoatUS Foundation fueling guidance (opens in a new tab).

If fuel spills but has not ignited
Stop the flow of fuel and notify the marina attendant immediately.
Do not start the engine or operate electrical switches in the affected area.
Keep people away from the spill and eliminate every possible ignition source.
Allow marina personnel to deploy oil-absorbent pads or containment booms.
Never use soap or detergent to make a sheen disappear. It spreads the contamination through the water and is illegal.
Report a spill that creates a sheen to the U.S. Coast Guard National Response Center at 1-800-424-8802, along with any required state or local notification.

BoatUS Foundation spill-response guidance (opens in a new tab)

If the fuel ignites
Shout a warning and get everyone away from the fuel dock immediately.
Call 911 from a safe location and clearly report that fuel is burning on the water.
Activate the fuel-dock emergency shutoff only if it can be reached without approaching the flames or passing through smoke.
Use the dock as the primary escape route when it remains safe. Do not automatically jump into the water—burning fuel can spread across the surface, and marina water may also present electrical hazards.
Do not start or move a burning boat unless emergency personnel direct you to do so.
Attempt to use a properly rated fire extinguisher only when the fire is still small, you know how to use it and you have a clear escape route behind you.
Never throw water onto burning gasoline. Leave a spreading fuel or marina fire to trained responders.

Boat and marina fires can spread quickly, so evacuation takes priority over saving the boat or fighting a growing fire. U.S. Fire Ad

mainText:
FloatPlanWizard
